dialogue.speaker: أَحْمَد
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you, how are you?

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.arabic: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ، بِخَيْر الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ.
dialogue.transliteration: w 3alaykum assalaam w ra7ma allah, bikhayr il7amdulillah.
dialogue.english: And upon you be peace and God's mercy, well, praise be to God.

dialogue.speaker: أَحْمَد
dialogue.english: How many people in your family?

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.english: I have my brother and two sisters.

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.arabic: أَخِي فِي الرِّيَاض، وَالْكُبْرَى فِي جِدَّة.
dialogue.transliteration: akhi fi Riyadh, w al-kubra fi Jidda.
dialogue.english: My brother is in Riyadh, and my older sister is in Jeddah.

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.transliteration: ee, 3indi zawji w waladi w binti.
dialogue.english: Yes, I have my husband and a son and a daughter.

dialogue.speaker: أَحْمَد
dialogue.arabic: لَا، مِتْزَوِّج، إِن شَاءَ اللَّهُ بِخَيْر.
dialogue.transliteration: la, mitzawwij, in sha2 allah bikhayr.

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.english: Praise be to God. What's your son's name?

pair.english: How many people in your family?

response.english: I have my brother and two sisters.
Yes, I have my husband and a daughter.

lessons.culture: In Hejazi families, asking about relatives is a warm and immediate greeting, and people share family news openly. The greeting "السّلام عليكم" is used regularly among locals and visitors alike. Being married or single is discussed openly, and single status followed by "إن شاء الله" (God willing) is the respectful way to discuss future marriage prospects, reflecting religious and traditional values.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟" Say you have a brother and two sisters.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; everyday Hejazi speech uses "عندي" and the colloquial forms.

exercises.tip: "عندي" is the everyday way to say what you have, including family members.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "My mother."

too_formal.feedback: This is the formal written term; everyday Hejazi speech says "أمي".

exercises.tip: "أمي" and "أبوي" are the everyday words for mother and father.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "My father."

too_formal.feedback: This is the formal written term; everyday Hejazi speech says "أبوي".

exercises.tip: The ending "-وي" here means "my" in Hejazi speech.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "my sister"?

too_formal.feedback: This is a more formal word for sister than the everyday "أختي".

exercises.tip: "أخوي" is my brother, "أختي" is my sister.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عِنْدِي أَخِي وَ_____." Meaning: I have a brother and two sisters.

too_formal.feedback: This is the formal dual form; everyday Hejazi speech says "ختين".

exercises.tip: "ختين" is the everyday Hejazi dual form for two sisters.

exercises.prompt: A man asks you: "إِنْتِ مِتْزَوِّجَة؟" (You are a woman.) Say yes, you have a husband and a daughter.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct but formal; everyday Hejazi speech says "عندي".

exercises.tip: "زوجي" is husband, "مرتي" is wife, and "عندي" is the everyday way to say you have someone.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "أَهْلِك / نَاسِ / كَمْ؟"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; the everyday spoken question is much shorter.

exercises.tip: The spoken pattern is "كم ناس" for "how many people".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm still single." (male speaker)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Hejazi speech says "لسا أعزب".

exercises.tip: "لسا" means "still" and is used constantly in everyday Hejazi speech.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "my husband"?

too_formal.feedback: This is the formal unmarked form; everyday Hejazi speech includes the possessive: "زوجي".

exercises.tip: "زوجي" is husband (with my), "مرتي" is wife (with my).

exercises.prompt: Complete: "إِيشْ اسْمِ _____؟" Meaning: What's your daughter's name? (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: The word "بنت" covers both "girl" and "daughter" in everyday Hejazi speech.

exercises.tip: "بنت" covers both "girl" and "daughter" in everyday Hejazi speech.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How many people are in your family?" (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is a formal, written-style question; the everyday spoken version is much shorter.

exercises.tip: "كم ناس" is a simple, direct way to ask "how many people".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "وَيْنِ أَخُوك هَسَّع؟" about your brother. Say he is in Riyadh.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; the everyday spoken answer is much shorter.

exercises.tip: A short place-name answer is natural and expected in casual Hejazi speech.

reply.english: Thank you. (may God give you well-being; the fixed reply)
Thank you. (may God give you well-being; the fixed reply)

dialogue.speaker: سَالِم
dialogue.english: I'm very hungry, I want to eat something.

dialogue.speaker: نُور
dialogue.english: What do you like to eat?

dialogue.speaker: نُور
dialogue.english: Okay, and what do you want to drink?

pair.english: What do you like to eat?

lessons.culture: Hejazi hospitality is generous, and hosts take pride in serving coffee and food to guests. The phrases "صحة وعافية" after someone finishes eating, and "بالعافية" while they are still eating, are always used and answered with "الله يعافيك". In the holy cities, religious phrases like "الحمد لله" (thank God) after eating are part of everyday courtesy, and people say "فوري" (right away) when serving or responding to requests.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm hungry." (male speaker)

too_formal.feedback: This is standard formal Arabic; everyday Hejazi speech says "جوعان".

exercises.tip: "جوعان" for a man, "جوعانة" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want to eat something."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; everyday Hejazi speech uses "ابي" directly before the verb.

exercises.tip: "ابي" plus a verb is the everyday pattern for "I want to...".

exercises.prompt: Which phrase is said to someone after they finish eating or drinking?

too_formal.feedback: This is a more elaborate, formal-sounding wish than the short fixed phrase "صحة وعافية".

exercises.tip: "بالعافية" is said while the meal is ongoing; "صحة وعافية" comes after.

exercises.prompt: Someone says "بِالْعَافِيَة" to you while you are eating. Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is a generic formal thanks; the fixed spoken reply here is "الله يعافيك".

exercises.tip: "بالعافية" and "الله يعافيك" are a fixed pair.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أَبِي _____ مَي." Meaning: I want to drink water.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; everyday speech simply says "ابي اشرب".

exercises.tip: After "ابي", the verb comes in its plain present form: "ابي اشرب". Water is "ماي".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "إِيشْ تِحِبّ تَاكُل؟" Say you like falafel.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct but more formal than the everyday "أحب".

exercises.tip: In Hejazi Arabic "أحب" is said as it is, with no extra prefix.

exercises.prompt: Someone says "صِحَّة وَعَافِيَة" to you after you finish eating. Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is a generic formal thanks rather than the fixed spoken reply "الله يعافيك".

exercises.tip: "صحة وعافية" and "الله يعافيك" are a fixed pair, said after eating or drinking.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The bill, please."

too_formal.feedback: This uses the more formal "الفاتورة" and "من فضلك"; everyday Hejazi speech says "الحساب".

exercises.tip: "الحساب" is the everyday word for the bill at a restaurant.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How much is the bill?"

too_formal.feedback: This is a formal written question; the everyday spoken version is much shorter.

exercises.tip: "كم" alone is the everyday way to ask the price.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "تَاكُل / تِحِبّ / إِيشْ؟"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic rather than the everyday spoken question.

exercises.tip: The question word comes first: "إيش + تحب + تاكل؟"

exercises.prompt: Which word means "thirsty" for a man?

too_formal.feedback: This is the classical/formal word for thirsty; everyday Hejazi speech says "عطشان".

exercises.tip: "جوعان" is hungry, "عطشان" is thirsty.

challenge.title: Meeting Family Over a Meal
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Hejazi conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include a question about someone's family, a description of at least one relative, a statement of hunger or thirst, ordering or offering food and drink, one of the fixed exchanges (بِالْعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك or صِحَّة وَعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك), and asking for the bill. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 2 and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A question about family using كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟ or similar.
A description of at least one family member using أمي, أبوي, أخوي, أختي, زوجي, مرتي, ولدي, or بنتي.
A statement of hunger or thirst using جوعان, جوعانة, or عطشان.
An order or offer of food or drink using أبي آكل or أبي اشرب.
One of the fixed exchanges: بِالْعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك, or صِحَّة وَعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك.
A request for the bill using الْحِسَاب لَوْ سَمَحْت or كَمْ الْحِسَاب؟
Both a masculine-address form (such as كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟) and a feminine-address form (such as كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟).
